summary:
I built PyroSync, a web-based Burning Activity Calendar and map that brings together five years (2021–2025) of NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS fire data for Pakistan.

Raw MODIS and VIIRS records usually conflict because VIIRS detects smaller fires at higher resolution, uses different confidence labels, and both sensors repeatedly flag stationary industrial gas flares. To fix this, I wrote a Python script to clean and align both datasets onto a single ~1 km grid, filter out persistent heat sources, and merge duplicate detections from the same day. On the dashboard, users can switch years, toggle between Harmonized, MODIS, and VIIRS views, and click any date to inspect fire hotspots on the map.

Having one clean timeline makes it much easier to track real seasonal burning spikes without sensor bias distorting the data.
details:
I built PyroSync completely Solo, with the help of SI, to solve a real headache when working with NASA's satellite fire data: trying to combine MODIS and VIIRS records without messing up historical fire trends.

How it works and what I had to account for If you just dump raw MODIS (1 km resolution) and VIIRS (375 m resolution) CSV files together, the numbers get skewed fast. VIIRS picks up smaller fires and often splits one fire into several detections, the two sensors label confidence differently (MODIS uses 0–100% while VIIRS uses low, nominal, and high), and both satellites repeatedly log stationary heat sources like gas flares and factories.

To fix this, I wrote a Python script (harmonize.py using pandas and numpy) that processes five years (2021–2025) of NASA FIRMS data for Pakistan:

  • First, it converts both confidence formats onto the same 0.0 to 1.0 scale and drops low-confidence noise below 0.40.
  • Next, it filters out static non-fire heat sources—any grid cell that triggers on more than 45 separate days across the dataset gets removed.
  • Then, it snaps same-day MODIS and VIIRS detections onto a shared ~1 km (0.01 degree) grid, keeps the highest Fire Radiative Power (FRP), and labels points spotted by both sensors (MODIS+VIIRS).
  • Finally, it flags critical burning days whenever daily FRP spikes well above the multi-year average.

Why this design and how it helps Instead of making users dig through massive spreadsheets, I built a 12-month Burning Activity Calendar connected to a live map. You can switch between years (2021–2025), flip between Harmonized, MODIS Raw, and VIIRS Raw modes to see how each sensor behaves on its own, and click any day on the calendar to inspect individual hotspots and FRP values on the map. My goal is to give researchers, local planners, and response teams a cleaner way to spot real seasonal burning spikes—like crop residue burning—without sensor differences throwing off the data.

Tools I used

  • Python (pandas, numpy) for cleaning and harmonizing the CSV archives
  • HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Leaflet.js (with Esri Dark Gray map tiles) for the dashboard
  • VS Code, Git/GitHub, and Netlify to host the pre-processed JSON and web app so it loads fast in any browser without needing a backend server
